html:
The Tuʻi Tonga were the sacred paramount chiefs of Tonga, whose influence reached across much of western Polynesia from about 950 CE, peaking between 1200 and 1500. Their capital was Muʻa on the island of Tongatapu.

Historians argue over the word "empire". What is clear from Tongan genealogies, oral history and archaeology is a network of power and exchange spread over hundreds of kilometres of sea. Tonga sat at the heart of the region the Lapita voyagers had settled two thousand years before, with close ties to Samoa, Fiji, ʻUvea (Wallis) and other islands. Marriages between chiefly families, tribute, and the exchange of fine mats, canoes and red feathers bound them together, sometimes backed by war canoes.

Remains of that power:

  • The langi, great stone-faced royal tombs at Muʻa.
  • The Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, a stone trilithon of about 1200.
  • Stone and pottery traded between islands, and Tongan words and titles found in neighbouring archipelagos.

Over time the Tuʻi Tonga became more sacred and less active in daily rule. From the 15th century a second line, the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, took over worldly power, and later a third, the Tuʻi Kanokupolu. James Cook visited in the 1770s and named Tonga the Friendly Islands. In the 19th century the Tuʻi Kanokupolu George Tupou I united Tonga as a kingdom, and the old Tuʻi Tonga title ended in 1865. Tonga was a British protectorate from 1900 to 1970 but never a colony.
